nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: High N requirement: typical rate 150–200 lb N/acre for grain production in the Southeast, depending on yield goal and soil organic matter.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Corn is one of the most N-demanding row crops. Residue has moderate C:N ratio (~40–60:1) and decomposes relatively quickly.

residue.description: High stover volume, relatively persistent through winter but decomposes more rapidly than cereal rye straw.

crops.rootSystem: Fibrous, relatively shallow compared with taproot crops.

pollinationSilking.note: Pollination and silking typically occur in July–August in Northern Hemisphere temperate regions (January–February in Southern Hemisphere). Heat stress above 35 °C and moisture deficits during this window can reduce kernel set.
pollinationSilking.source: NC State Extension Corn Production Guide / FAO Crop Calendar

growingWindow.description: Warm-season cereal grain planted in spring (April–May in Northern Hemisphere, October–November in Southern Hemisphere Pampas/Cerrado, or onset of rains in tropical highlands/subhumid zones).

diseasePestNotes: Corn residue can harbor Fusarium species that may affect subsequent small-grain crops.
Rootworm and cutworm management may be needed in continuous-corn systems.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Corn Production Guide
FAO Crop Calendar & CIMMYT Maize Agronomy
Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences (CAAS) Maize Systems

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Fixes atmospheric N via Bradyrhizobium symbiosis when effectively nodulated. Most fixed N is sequestered in crop biomass and removed with grain harvest.

residualNcredit.note: NC State Extension estimates approximately 15–30 lb N/acre as a residual nitrogen credit following soybean. This is a contextual estimate, not a guaranteed field-specific amount.
residualNcredit.source: NC State Extension Soybean Production Guide

nitrogenBehavior.note: Soybean grain exports substantial nitrogen. Do not treat all biological N fixation as a next-crop fertilizer replacement.

residue.description: Relatively low-residue profile compared with corn or small grains; residue decomposes readily.

crops.rootSystem: Taproot with extensive lateral branching.

podFill.note: Pod fill and seed development typically occur August–September in Northern Hemisphere (February–March in Southern Hemisphere). Moisture stress and prolonged heat can reduce seed size and yield.
podFill.source: NC State Extension Soybean Production Guide / EMBRAPA Soja

growingWindow.description: Warm-season oilseed legume planted May–June in North America, China, and Europe, or October–December in South American Pampas/Cerrado.

diseasePestNotes: Soybean cyst nematode (SCN, Heterodera glycines) can build populations in continuous or frequent soybean rotations.
White mold (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum) risk increases in cool, wet conditions and with tight rotations involving other susceptible hosts.
Moderate non-host break intervals help manage SCN.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Soybean Production Guide
CAAS Institute of Crop Sciences & EMBRAPA Soybean Systems
IITA Tropical Soybean Improvement Program

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Moderate N requirement; timing is important (split applications in spring).
nitrogenBehavior.note: Straw residues have high C:N ratio and can contribute to soil organic matter but may temporarily immobilize N if incorporated fresh.

residue.description: Significant straw biomass after grain harvest; provides ground-cover value if left on the surface.

crops.rootSystem: Fibrous root system that develops in fall and resumes growth in spring.

grainFill.note: Grain filling and maturity occur in May–June for Northern Hemisphere winter wheat (October–November in Southern Hemisphere).
grainFill.source: NC State Extension Small Grain Production Guide / FAO Crop Calendar

growingWindow.description: Planted in autumn (October–November in US, North China Plain, and Europe; May–June in South America), vernalizes over winter, and harvests in early summer.

diseasePestNotes: Fusarium head blight (scab) risk can increase when wheat follows corn or sorghum due to shared Fusarium inoculum in residue.
Hessian fly and rust diseases should be monitored.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Small Grain Production Guide
CAAS North China Plain Winter Wheat–Summer Maize Double-Cropping Guide
CIMMYT Global Wheat Program

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Moderate N requirement, generally somewhat less per unit yield than corn.
nitrogenBehavior.note: High-biomass stover residue can contribute organic matter but may carry Fusarium inoculum affecting subsequent small grains.

residue.description: High-biomass stover that can improve soil coverage but decomposes more slowly than corn stover.

crops.rootSystem: Fibrous, deep rooting capacity under drought stress.

grainFill.note: Grain filling typically occurs in August–September in Northern Hemisphere. Sorghum is more drought-resilient than corn during this period.

growingWindow.description: Warm-season drought-tolerant cereal planted May–June in North America, China, and Mediterranean/MENA, or October–November in Australia and South America.

diseasePestNotes: Fusarium head blight risk to subsequent wheat should be considered.
Sorghum can host some pests shared with corn.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Sorghum Production
USDA ARS & University of Nevada Extension Water-Limited Grain Systems
GRDC Australia Northern Region Sorghum Guide

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Moderate N requirement; deep taproot can scavenge nutrients from lower soil profiles.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Can extract water and nutrients from deeper soil layers due to taproot architecture.

residue.description: Moderate residue from stalks and heads; persistent through winter.

crops.rootSystem: Deep taproot that can extend below the typical corn root zone.

flowering.note: Flowering typically occurs in July–August in Northern Hemisphere. Heat stress and moisture deficits can reduce oil content in oil-type varieties.

growingWindow.description: Deep-rooted broadleaf oilseed planted May–June in Northern Hemisphere or October–November in Southern Hemisphere.

diseasePestNotes: Sclerotinia head rot and white mold are concerns; sunflower and soybean can both be hosts associated with Sclerotinia sclerotiorum.
A short rotation interval may not provide an adequate disease break for Sclerotinia. Extension guidance recommends managing field history and variety selection.

sources.citation: USDA NASS Sunflower Production
NC State Extension Plant Pathology — Sclerotinia
FAO Crop Calendar — Sunflower (Helianthus annuus)

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Nitrogen scavenger. Can temporarily immobilize available nitrogen due to high C:N ratio in residue.
nitrogenBehavior.immobilizationRisk: Rye terminated at late boot or past can have C:N ratios >40:1, temporarily tying up available N in spring. Early termination reduces immobilization risk.
nitrogenBehavior.source: NC State Extension Organic Grains — Cover Crops

residue.description: High biomass and very persistent residue that provides excellent soil coverage and erosion protection.

crops.rootSystem: Dense, fibrous root system that scavenges available nutrients.

growingWindow.description: Winter-hardy cereal cover crop planted in autumn and terminated in spring prior to cash crop planting.

diseasePestNotes: Generally low disease concerns, but can host some nematodes if grown continuously.
Late termination can reduce spring soil moisture available for the next cash crop.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Organic Grains — Cover Crops
USDA NRCS Cover Crop Termination Guidelines

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Legume cover crop that can contribute nitrogen to the following crop.

residualNcredit.note: NC State Extension reports approximately 60–75 lb N/acre following crimson clover. Actual contribution depends on biomass production, maturity at termination, and growing conditions.
residualNcredit.source: NC State Extension Winter Annual Cover Crops

nitrogenBehavior.note: N contribution varies with biomass, maturity, termination timing, and growing conditions. Do not treat as a guaranteed fertilizer replacement.

residue.description: Soft residue that decomposes relatively quickly compared with cereal rye.

crops.rootSystem: Shallow taproot with some nitrogen fixation nodules.

growingWindow.description: Winter legume cover crop planted in autumn and terminated in spring before full bloom for maximum N contribution.

diseasePestNotes: Generally low disease pressure; provides break from grass-family diseases.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Winter Annual Cover Crops

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Legume cover crop with high nitrogen-fixation potential.

residualNcredit.note: NC State Extension reports approximately 80–100 lb N/acre following hairy vetch. Actual contribution depends on biomass, maturity, termination timing, and growing conditions.
residualNcredit.source: NC State Extension Winter Annual Cover Crops

nitrogenBehavior.note: Volunteer growth can be an issue if seed is allowed to mature. Termination timing affects both N contribution and volunteer management.

residue.description: Viny residue that provides moderate soil coverage; decomposes faster than cereal rye.

crops.rootSystem: Deep taproot with N-fixing nodules.

growingWindow.description: Winter-hardy legume cover crop planted September–October and terminated in spring across temperate, continental, and Mediterranean systems.

diseasePestNotes: May harbor some pests if not rotated; generally beneficial as a break crop.
Volunteer hairy vetch can become a weed in subsequent crops if allowed to set seed.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Winter Annual Cover Crops
ICARDA & CAAS Cool-Season Legume Cover Systems

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Nitrogen scavenger; bio-drilling effect from deep taproot can improve compaction layers but does not fix atmospheric N.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Can scavenge residual N from lower soil profiles, making it available to subsequent shallow-rooted crops.

residue.description: Can winter-kill in temperate zones, leaving minimal spring living cover. Tissue decomposes rapidly.

crops.rootSystem: Deep taproot (bio-drill) that can penetrate compacted subsoil layers; typically winter-kills.

growingWindow.description: Planted late summer–early fall; penetrates compacted layers and scavenges residual profile nitrogen.

diseasePestNotes: Can host clubroot if Brassica diseases are present in the field history.
Winter-kill behavior means less spring erosion protection than living cover crops.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Small Farms — Winter Crops

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Warm-season biomass producer and nutrient scavenger.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Rapid growth in summer heat; can produce significant biomass for grazing or soil coverage.

residue.description: Significant warm-season biomass; stems are moderately persistent.

crops.rootSystem: Fibrous, dense root system that improves soil structure.

growingWindow.description: Warm-season drought-tolerant grass cover crop planted after small-grain harvest or as a rapid soil-building cover.

diseasePestNotes: Generally resistant to many diseases that affect corn and sorghum.
Provides a beneficial break from grass-family diseases when rotated with corn or sorghum.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Summer Annual Forages
ICRISAT Pearl Millet Agronomy

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Nitrogen scavenger; moderate C:N ratio compared with cereal rye.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Less persistent residue than cereal rye; decomposes more readily.

residue.description: Moderate biomass that winter-kills in colder temperate zones, providing spring residue cover.

crops.rootSystem: Fibrous root system that provides some soil stabilization.

growingWindow.description: Cool-season grass cover crop providing rapid autumn ground cover and erosion control.

diseasePestNotes: Generally low disease pressure; can host some cereal diseases at low levels.
Winter-kill means less spring coverage than living cover crops like cereal rye or crimson clover.

sources.citation: NC State Extension Small Farms — Winter Crops

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Moderate N demand (40–80 kg N/ha in rainfed Sudano-Sahelian and semi-arid tropical systems); benefits strongly from preceding cowpea or groundnut rotation.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Crop stover has moderately high C:N ratio; rotating with N-fixing pulses (cowpea, groundnut, pigeon pea) restores topsoil mineralizable N.

residue.description: Abundant stalk and leaf residue that protects tropical savanna soils against wind and early-rain splash erosion when retained as surface mulch.

crops.rootSystem: Deep, dense fibrous root system extending 1.5–2.0 m to extract subsoil moisture during intra-seasonal dry spells.

floweringGrainFill.note: Booting, flowering, and grain fill occur in August–September during peak/late rainy season in Northern Hemisphere Sudano-Sahelian savannas.
floweringGrainFill.source: ICRISAT Sorghum Improvement Program & FAO Crop Calendar

growingWindow.description: Primary staple cereal of the Sudano-Sahelian and East/Southern African savanna zones, planted with the onset of dependable rains (May–July in Bahr el Ghazal / Darfur / Sahel) and harvested in October–November.

diseasePestNotes: Continuous sorghum builds parasitic witchweed (Striga hermonthica) seedbanks; rotation with trap/non-host crops (cowpea, groundnut, sesame, soybean) is essential.
Anthracnose and grain mold pressure increase in humid late seasons.

sources.citation: ICRISAT — Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) Rainfed Savanna Production Systems
FAO Crop Calendar — Sudan & South Sudan Sorghum Cropping Zones

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Low-to-moderate N demand (30–60 kg N/ha); well adapted to low-fertility sandy Alfisols and Arenosols when rotated with cowpea or groundnut.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Efficient nutrient scavenger in sandy-loam savanna soils.

residue.description: Tough stalks provide critical dry-season windbreak and surface mulch against Sahelian/Sudanian soil crusting.

crops.rootSystem: Rapidly penetrating deep fibrous root system capable of reaching 1.8 m within 60 days.

panicleFlowering.note: Flowering and grain set in August–September; highly heat-tolerant up to 40 °C.

growingWindow.description: Short-duration (75–100 day) drought-hardy grain cereal planted across Sudano-Sahelian Africa and semi-arid South Asia.

diseasePestNotes: Downy mildew (Sclerospora graminicola) and Striga hermonthica build under continuous millet monoculture; rotate with legumes (cowpea, groundnut) and sesame.
Head miner and bird pressure require timely harvest.

sources.citation: ICRISAT — Pearl Millet Production in Semi-Arid Tropics
FAO Crop Calendar — Pearl Millet (Pennisetum glaucum)

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Symbiotic N2 fixer via Bradyrhizobium; fixes 40–90 kg N/ha and provides a net positive residual nitrogen credit to subsequent sorghum, millet, or maize.

residualNcredit.note: IITA and ICRISAT rotation trials report 35–60 kg N/ha fertilizer replacement value for cereal crops following grain cowpea when haulms are retained.

nitrogenBehavior.note: Retaining vine residue on the field maximizes N transfer to the next cereal crop.

residue.description: Nitrogen-rich leafy vines that cover the soil during the rainy season and mineralize rapidly at the start of the following season.

crops.rootSystem: Deep taproot with drought-tolerant nodulated lateral roots.

floweringPodSet.note: Flowering and pod fill in August–October; excess waterlogging reduces nodulation.

growingWindow.description: Heat- and drought-adapted grain legume grown across Sudano-Sahelian Africa, East/Southern Africa, South Asia, and tropical Americas.

diseasePestNotes: Acts as a non-host trap crop that induces suicidal germination of Striga hermonthica, breaking parasitic weed cycles in sorghum/millet rotations.
Pod borers (Maruca vitrata), thrips, and macrophomina charcoal rot increase if cowpea is grown in back-to-back years.

sources.citation: International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) — Cowpea
ICRISAT & FAO Crop Calendar — Vigna unguiculata

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Biological nitrogen fixer (fixes 50–110 kg N/ha); leaves mineralizable N in root/haulm residues for following cereals.

residualNcredit.note: Documented residual N credit to subsequent sorghum, millet, maize, or wheat when haulms are not completely exported.
residualNcredit.source: ICRISAT Groundnut Production & CAAS Oilseed Systems

nitrogenBehavior.note: Requires adequate topsoil calcium and friable sandy-loam to loam surface texture for peg penetration.

residue.description: High-protein haulm residue decomposes rapidly; pairing with a post-harvest cover crop or retaining cereal stover protects soil.

crops.rootSystem: Deep taproot (up to 1.3 m) with abundant N-fixing nodules in the upper 30 cm.

peggingPodFill.note: Pegging and pod fill (July–September in NH rainy season) are sensitive to severe late-season drought, which elevates aflatoxin risk.

growingWindow.description: Major oilseed and food legume across Sudano-Sahelian Africa (Sudan, South Sudan, Nigeria, Senegal), China, South/Southeast Asia, and the Americas.

diseasePestNotes: Early and late leaf spot (Cercospora), rosette virus, and Aspergillus flavus require a minimum 1–2 year cereal/oilseed break.
Suppresses Striga hermonthica and cereal root pathogens when rotated with sorghum, millet, or maize.

sources.citation: ICRISAT — Groundnut (Arachis hypogaea) Improvement & Agronomy
CAAS Oil Crops Research Institute & FAO Crop Calendar

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Low-to-moderate N demand (30–50 kg N/ha); deep root system scavenges subsoil nutrients unused by shallow fibrous crops.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Non-legume broadleaf oilseed (Pedaliaceae) that provides a distinct botanical family break from both Poaceae cereals and Fabaceae pulses.

residue.description: Erect woody stems leave standing stubble that reduces wind erosion during the dry season.

crops.rootSystem: Deep taproot with extensive secondary fibrous roots that improve soil macroporosity and water infiltration.

floweringCapsuleFill.note: Flowering and capsule development in August–September; highly drought-tolerant once established but sensitive to prolonged waterlogging.
floweringCapsuleFill.source: FAO Crop Calendar & Sudan ARC Sesame Production Guide

growingWindow.description: Signature drought-tolerant cash oilseed of the Sudan/South Sudan savanna belt, East Africa, South Asia, and China.

diseasePestNotes: Belongs to Pedaliaceae, breaking root-knot nematode, Striga, and cereal/legume pathogen cycles.
Fusarium wilt and webworm (Antigastra catalaunalis) require rotating sesame with cereals and legumes rather than back-to-back sesame.

sources.citation: FAO Crop Calendar — Sesamum indicum (Sudan, South Sudan, East Africa, Asia)
ICRISAT & Regional Dryland Oilseed Cropping Systems

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: High biological N2 fixation (60–120 kg N/ha) plus substantial leaf-fall litter that enriches topsoil organic N and solubilizes bound soil phosphorus.

residualNcredit.note: ICRISAT long-term trials demonstrate 40–75 kg N/ha residual N credit to subsequent sorghum, maize, or millet from shed leaves and root turnover.

nitrogenBehavior.note: Root exudates (piscidic acid) mobilize iron-bound phosphorus in tropical Alfisols, Ultisols, and Oxisols.

residue.description: Heavy leaf drop builds surface organic matter while woody stems provide fuel/mulch.

crops.rootSystem: Very deep woody taproot (2.0+ m) that breaks subsoil hardpans ('biological plow') and accesses deep moisture into the dry season.

floweringPodFill.note: Flowers and fills pods at the end of the rainy season into early dry season using residual deep soil moisture.

growingWindow.description: Medium-duration drought-resilient grain legume grown across Sudano-Sahelian & East/Southern Africa, South Asia, and tropical South America.

diseasePestNotes: Fusarium udum wilt builds if pigeon pea is repeated without a 2-year cereal/oilseed break.
Deep taproot and leaf litter strongly suppress Striga and improve subsequent cereal yields.

sources.citation: ICRISAT — Pigeonpea (Cajanus cajan) Improvement Program
FAO Crop Calendar — Cajanus cajan

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Moderate N and high K uptake by storage roots; benefits strongly from rotation with N-fixing grain or cover legumes (cowpea, groundnut, sunn hemp).
nitrogenBehavior.note: Returning leafy tops to the soil recycles a large fraction of assimilated nitrogen.

residue.description: Woody stems and fallen foliage provide moderate post-harvest soil protection.

crops.rootSystem: Tuberous storage roots with deep fibrous feeder roots tolerant of acidic, low-phosphorus tropical soils.

growingWindow.description: Drought-resilient Euphorbiaceae root crop planted at rainy onset in humid, subhumid, and moist savanna zones of Africa, Southeast Asia, and South America.

diseasePestNotes: Euphorbiaceae family provides a complete botanical break from Poaceae cereal and Fabaceae legume pests.
Cassava mosaic disease (CMD) and bacterial blight require clean planting stakes and rotation with legumes/cereals.

sources.citation: IITA — Cassava (Manihot esculenta) Cropping Systems
FAO Save and Grow: Cassava & EMBRAPA Mandioca

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Rapid warm-season nitrogen-fixing cover crop producing 80–120 kg N/ha in 60–90 days.

residualNcredit.note: Terminating at early flowering before stems lignify releases substantial mineral N to the subsequent cash crop.
residualNcredit.source: USDA NRCS & IITA Tropical Green Manure Trials

nitrogenBehavior.note: Terminate within 60–75 days of planting to keep C:N ratio low and maximize N mineralization.

residue.description: Tall fibrous stalks and leafy canopy provide dense weed suppression and erosion protection.

crops.rootSystem: Deep taproot with large coralloid nitrogen-fixing nodules; suppresses root-knot and reniform nematodes.

growingWindow.planting: Late rainy / relay window (August–October in NH tropics; March–May in SH)
growingWindow.description: Fast-growing tropical and subtropical legume cover crop grown in early or late rainy windows across Africa, South/Southeast Asia, and Brazil.

diseasePestNotes: Produces pyrrolizidine compounds that actively suppress plant-parasitic nematodes (Meloidogyne and Rotylenchulus spp.) and Striga.
Low pest carryover to cereal or oilseed cash crops.

sources.citation: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Sunn Hemp (Crotalaria juncea)
IITA & EMBRAPA Green Manure Cover Crop Systems

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Drought-resilient post-rainy cover and forage legume fixing 50–100 kg N/ha on residual soil moisture.

residualNcredit.note: Widely grown as 'Lubia' in Sudan/South Sudan and East Africa as a soil-restoring rotational legume.
residualNcredit.source: ILRI / ICRISAT Tropical Forage & Cover Legumes

nitrogenBehavior.note: Stays green well into the dry season due to its deep taproot, protecting topsoil from wind erosion.

residue.description: Dense trailing vines form a thick living and dead mulch mat through the post-rainy dry transition.

crops.rootSystem: Deep, vigorous taproot reaching 2 m depth, extracting residual subsoil moisture after main rains end.

growingWindow.description: Post-rainy / relay cover crop ('Lubia') planted late in the wet season across Sudano-Sahelian and East African savannas, South Asia, and MENA.

diseasePestNotes: Suppresses Striga hermonthica and dry-season weed establishment when relayed after early millet, sorghum, or sesame.
Rotate away from other Fabaceae pulses in the main rainy season of the same year to avoid legume pest carryover.

sources.citation: ILRI & ICRISAT — Lablab purpureus ('Lubia') in Sudano-Sahelian & East African Farming Systems
FAO Grassland & Pasture Crop Profiles — Lablab purpureus

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Lower N and water requirement than wheat or corn (60–110 lb N/acre); excess N in malt barley is avoided to keep grain protein moderate.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Maturing 2–3 weeks earlier than wheat, barley escapes peak summer heat and drought stress in Nevada, the US West, Mediterranean, and MENA.

residue.description: Fine straw provides reliable surface cover against wind erosion in semi-arid and arid basins.

crops.rootSystem: Fibrous root system with superior salinity/alkalinity tolerance (up to pH 8.2) compared with other small grains.

headingGrainFill.note: Heading and grain fill occur in May–June in Northern Hemisphere spring/winter systems, completing before peak July–August heat.
headingGrainFill.source: University of Nevada Cooperative Extension & USDA ARS

growingWindow.description: Most drought- and salinity-tolerant temperate small grain, widely grown across Nevada/US Southwest, Great Plains, Northern China, Europe, Australia, and MENA.

diseasePestNotes: Cereal cyst nematode and net blotch require rotating with non-grass crops (alfalfa/medics, safflower, brassicas, or pulses).
Early harvest allows timely establishment of a summer or autumn cover crop.

sources.citation: University of Nevada Cooperative Extension — Small Grain Production in Nevada
ICARDA Dryland Barley Improvement & GRDC Barley Guide

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Requires 90–140 lb N/acre to achieve high bread/durum protein; benefits strongly from preceding alfalfa/medic, chickpea, or vetch N credits.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Straw residue protects soil surface against wind erosion in semi-arid valleys and plains.

residue.description: Durable cereal straw that conserves soil moisture and reduces evaporative loss.

crops.rootSystem: Deep fibrous root system reaching 1.2–1.5 m.

anthesisGrainFill.note: Flowering and grain fill occur in May–June (NH) or October–November (SH Australia).
anthesisGrainFill.source: University of Nevada Extension / CIMMYT / GRDC

growingWindow.description: Primary cereal grain across irrigated and dryland western US (Nevada, Great Plains), Northeast/Northwest China, Indo-Gangetic Plains, Australia, and MENA.

diseasePestNotes: Avoid planting immediately after corn or sorghum where Fusarium head blight pressure is high.
Rotate with broadleaf oilseeds (safflower, canola) and legumes (chickpea, lentil, medics/alfalfa) to break take-all and root rot cycles.

sources.citation: University of Nevada Cooperative Extension & USDA NASS Nevada Crop Statistics
CIMMYT, CAAS China & GRDC Australia Wheat Agronomy

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Moderate N demand (50–80 lb N/acre); deep taproot recovers leached nitrate from 1.5–2.5 m depth unreachable by small grains.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Excellent deep-profile nutrient and moisture scavenger in western US, Mediterranean, and semi-arid rotations.

residue.description: Stiff branched stalks remain upright over winter, trapping snow and reducing wind speed at the soil surface.

crops.rootSystem: Deepest taproot of annual oilseeds (penetrating 2.0–3.0 m), breaking subsoil compaction in arid and semi-arid valleys.

buddingFlowering.note: Flowering in June–July; thrives in dry sunny weather with low relative humidity.
buddingFlowering.source: University of Nevada Extension & USDA ARS Western Oilseed Guide

growingWindow.description: Deep-rooted drought- and salinity-tolerant Asteraceae oilseed adapted to Nevada/US Southwest, Great Plains, Northwest China, Australia, and MENA.

diseasePestNotes: Provides a non-host broadleaf break for cereal root diseases and nematodes in wheat/barley rotations.
Alternaria leaf blight and Phytophthora root rot require well-drained or carefully irrigated soils and a 2-year break between Asteraceae crops.

sources.citation: University of Nevada Cooperative Extension & USDA ARS — Safflower Production in the Intermountain West
GRDC Australia — Safflower Grownotes

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: High biological nitrogen fixation via Sinorhizobium meliloti (fixes 120–200 lb N/acre/yr under irrigated Nevada/Southwest conditions or 60–110 lb N/acre in dryland medic systems).

residualNcredit.note: University of Nevada Cooperative Extension and western land-grant guidelines document 70–120 lb N/acre first-year N credit to small grains or corn following alfalfa/medic termination.
residualNcredit.source: University of Nevada Cooperative Extension — Alfalfa & Forage Systems

nitrogenBehavior.note: Primary foundation crop of irrigated Nevada and Intermountain West agriculture.

residue.description: Dense crown and root biomass builds soil aggregate stability and organic matter.

crops.rootSystem: Deep taproot (2–4 m) with prolific nitrogen-fixing nodules; tolerates neutral-to-alkaline soils (pH 6.5–8.2) typical of Great Basin and Mediterranean soils.

growingWindow.description: Signature irrigated forage legume of Nevada and the US Southwest, as well as ley-farming medic rotations in Southern Australia, Mediterranean Europe, and MENA.

diseasePestNotes: Rotating out of alfalfa/medic into barley, wheat, or safflower breaks alfalfa weevil, stem nematode (Ditylenchus dipsaci), and autotoxicity.
Provides complete suppression of cereal root diseases.

sources.citation: University of Nevada Cooperative Extension — Nevada Alfalfa Production & Irrigation Management
GRDC & ICARDA Pasture Medic–Cereal Ley Rotation Systems

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Heat- and drought-tolerant N-fixing pulse legume; fixes 35–70 lb N/acre with low irrigation demand.

residualNcredit.note: Provides residual N credit and low water footprint ahead of winter/spring barley or wheat.
residualNcredit.source: USDA ARS Arid-Land Agricultural Research Center

nitrogenBehavior.note: Sets pods at daytime temperatures up to 38–40 °C where common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) aborts flowers.

residue.description: Fine vine residue that mineralizes quickly; best followed by a fall small grain or mustard cover crop.

crops.rootSystem: Deep, fine taproot system adapted to rapid moisture extraction in desert and semi-arid soils.

floweringPodFill.note: Flowering in July–August; uniquely tolerant of high vapor pressure deficits in the US Southwest.

growingWindow.description: Native Southwestern heat- and drought-adapted grain legume for water-limited irrigated and semi-arid rotations in Nevada and the US Southwest.

diseasePestNotes: High natural resistance to common bacterial blight and charcoal rot.
Breaks cereal pathogen cycles in barley, wheat, and sorghum rotations.

sources.citation: USDA ARS Arid-Land Agricultural Research Center — Tepary Bean (Phaseolus acutifolius)

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Rapid cool-season nitrate scavenger; captures 40–80 lb residual N/acre before winter leaching.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Glucosinolate compounds in root and shoot tissue provide natural biofumigation against soilborne fungi and nematodes.

residue.description: Fast canopy closure protects bare soil against autumn/spring wind erosion in western valleys and Mediterranean basins.

crops.rootSystem: Vigorous taproot with dense fine lateral roots in the upper 60 cm.

growingWindow.description: Fast-establishing Brassicaceae cover crop for US Southwest/Nevada, Mediterranean Europe, South Asia, Australia, and MENA.

diseasePestNotes: Provides a non-host Brassicaceae family break in cereal–legume–asteraceae rotations.
Do not plant immediately before or after canola/rapeseed to avoid shared Brassica clubroot or flea beetle pressure.

sources.citation: USDA NRCS Western Cover Crop Guide — White/Yellow Mustard (Sinapis alba)

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: High N demand (120–180 kg N/ha); flooded/anaerobic soil phase alters N dynamics and suppresses aerobic soilborne diseases for subsequent upland winter crops (wheat, canola, chickpea, or vetch).
nitrogenBehavior.note: Rice–winter wheat and rice–winter rapeseed (canola) or rice–mung bean/vetch are cornerstone rotations of the Yangtze Basin, Indo-Gangetic Plains, and Southeast Asia.

residue.description: High silica-rich straw volume providing strong surface mulch for subsequent zero-till wheat, canola, or pulses.

crops.rootSystem: Fibrous root system with aerenchyma adapted to saturated and lowland clay-loam soils.

bootingFlowering.note: Booting and flowering (July–August in NH monsoon/subtropical systems) are sensitive to water deficit and extreme heat (>36 °C).
bootingFlowering.source: CAAS China National Rice Research Institute & IRRI

growingWindow.description: Primary staple cereal of Southern/Central/Northeast China, South Asia (Indo-Gangetic Plains), and Southeast Asia.

diseasePestNotes: Flooded paddy phase eradicates many aerobic cyst nematodes and Sclerotinia sclerotia affecting upland broadleaf crops.
Rice blast and sheath blight are reduced by rotating with winter canola, winter wheat, chickpea, lentil, or hairy vetch.

sources.citation: CAAS China National Rice Research Institute & FAO Crop Calendar
IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank & ICAR Rice–Wheat Cropping Systems

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Moderate N demand (50–90 kg N/ha); responds strongly to preceding cowpea, groundnut, soybean, or sunn hemp N fixation.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Grown under aerobic rainfed conditions in moist savannas, subhumid tropics, and monsoon uplands.

residue.description: Straw mulch protects tropical upland soils against heavy rainfall impact.

crops.rootSystem: Deeper, thicker fibrous roots than lowland paddy varieties for aerobic moisture extraction.

growingWindow.description: Aerobic rainfed rice (including AfricaRice NERICA and EMBRAPA upland cultivars) grown in subhumid/moist savanna Africa, Southeast Asia, South Asia, and the Brazilian Cerrado.

diseasePestNotes: Aerobic upland rice must be rotated with legumes (cowpea, soybean, groundnut, pigeon pea) or cassava/sesame to prevent root-knot nematode and Striga buildup.
Rice blast pressure is mitigated by balanced N from legume residues.

sources.citation: AfricaRice — NERICA Upland Rice Cropping Systems
EMBRAPA Rice & Beans & IRRI Upland Rice

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: High autumn/spring N uptake with deep taproot scavenging; leaves friable soil structure and 20–30 kg N/ha mineralizable leaf-drop residue for following wheat or rice.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Premier broadleaf cash break crop in cereal-dominated rotations across China (Yangtze & Northern plains), Europe, Australia, South Asia, and North America.

residue.description: Branching stems and early-shed leaves improve surface tilth and biological activity.

crops.rootSystem: Strong taproot (1.2–1.8 m) that bio-drills plough pans and suppresses cereal take-all fungus (Gaeumannomyces graminis).

floweringPodFill.note: Flowering in April–May (NH winter crop) or August–September (SH Australia); avoids peak summer heat.
floweringPodFill.source: CAAS Oil Crops Research Institute & GRDC Canola Guide

growingWindow.planting: September–October (NH Winter) / April–May (NH Spring or SH Australia)
growingWindow.harvest: May–June (NH Winter) / August–September (NH Spring) / November (SH Australia)
growingWindow.description: Major Brassicaceae oilseed cash crop grown in rotation with rice, wheat, barley, corn, and pulses.

diseasePestNotes: Host of Sclerotinia stem rot (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum) and clubroot; do not plant in more than 1 year of a 3-year rotation or stack with soybean/sunflower.
Root glucosinolates suppress cereal take-all and root lesion nematodes, boosting subsequent wheat yields by 10–20%.

sources.citation: CAAS Oil Crops Research Institute — Yangtze & Northern Rapeseed Systems
GRDC Australia Canola Grownotes & FAO Crop Calendar

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Symbiotic N2 fixer via Mesorhizobium ciceri (fixes 40–90 kg N/ha); provides a reliable residual N credit to subsequent wheat, barley, sorghum, or rice.

residualNcredit.note: ICRISAT, ICARDA, and GRDC document 35–60 kg N/ha fertilizer savings for wheat/barley following chickpea.

nitrogenBehavior.note: Thrives on stored post-rainy (Rabi) soil moisture or cool winter-wet Mediterranean rainfall.

residue.description: Organic acid-rich foliage decomposes quickly; retain cereal straw in the system for surface cover.

crops.rootSystem: Deep taproot (1.2–1.5 m) capable of extracting receding subsoil moisture during post-rainy grain fill.

floweringPodSet.note: Flowering in February–March (Rabi/Mediterranean) or May–June (NH spring); chilling (<10 °C) or extreme heat (>35 °C) during flowering reduces pod set.

growingWindow.planting: October–November (Rabi / Mediterranean / East Africa Highlands) or April–May (Australia / NH Spring)
growingWindow.description: Premier drought-tolerant cool-season pulse crop across South Asia, MENA, Mediterranean Europe, Southern Australia, East African highlands, and the western US.

diseasePestNotes: Ascochyta blight and Fusarium oxysporum wilt require rotating with cereals and oilseeds with at least a 2-year interval between chickpea crops.
Breaks cereal root lesion nematode (Pratylenchus thornei) and take-all cycles in wheat/barley rotations.

sources.citation: ICRISAT — Chickpea (Cicer arietinum) Global Research
ICARDA & GRDC Chickpea Production Guides

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Fixes 35–75 kg N/ha via Rhizobium leguminosarum and leaves higher soil water reserves for subsequent wheat or barley than deep-depleting oilseeds.

residualNcredit.note: ICARDA Mediterranean and dryland trials document both residual N and conserved subsoil water benefits for wheat/barley following lentil.

nitrogenBehavior.note: Shallow-to-moderate root depth conserves deeper profile water for the next cereal crop.

residue.description: Delicate stems decompose rapidly; pair with high-residue cereals or brassica cover crops.

crops.rootSystem: Slender taproot (0.6–0.9 m) densely nodulated in the topsoil.

growingWindow.planting: October–December (MENA / Mediterranean / South Asia) or April–May (Australia / Northern Plains)
growingWindow.harvest: March–May (South Asia / MENA) / July–August (NH Spring) / November (Australia)
growingWindow.description: Cool-season drought-hardy pulse staple of MENA, Mediterranean Europe, South Asia, Australia, East African highlands, and Northern Plains.

diseasePestNotes: Broomrape (Orobanche) and Fusarium wilt require a 2-year non-host break with cereals and brassicas/oilseeds.
Disrupts cereal root rot and grassy weed cycles.

sources.citation: ICARDA — Lentil (Lens culinaris) Dryland Cropping Systems
FAO Crop Calendar & GRDC Lentil Grownotes

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Ultra-short-duration (60–75 day) N-fixing grain legume fixing 30–60 kg N/ha in summer/catch-crop windows between main cereal harvests.

residualNcredit.note: CAAS, ICAR, and ICRISAT document 30–45 kg N/ha credit when mung bean pods are picked and green haulms are incorporated before rice or wheat.

nitrogenBehavior.note: Fits short summer or post-rainy windows without delaying main cereal planting.

residue.description: Green haulms mineralize rapidly, releasing plant-available N within 2–3 weeks.

crops.rootSystem: Nodulated taproot reaching 0.8–1.0 m.

growingWindow.planting: June–July (China/Temperate Summer) or March–May (South/SE Asia pre-monsoon) or October–November (SH)
growingWindow.harvest: August–September or May–July (60–75 days after planting)
growingWindow.description: Short-season heat-tolerant pulse widely grown in Northern & Southern China, South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Africa, and Australia.

diseasePestNotes: Breaks cereal pest cycles in wheat–rice and wheat–maize systems.
Mungbean yellow mosaic virus and Cercospora leaf spot are managed through rotation with cereals and brassicas.

sources.citation: CAAS Institute of Crop Sciences — Mung Bean (Vigna radiata) in Chinese Rotations
ICAR & World Vegetable Center / ICRISAT Mungbean Agronomy

nitrogenBehavior.demandCategory: Low N requirement; root exudates solubilize calcium- and aluminum-bound soil phosphorus, making P available to subsequent crops.
nitrogenBehavior.note: Belongs to Polygonaceae, adding a 4th or 5th distinct botanical family to cereal–legume–brassica rotations.

residue.description: Establishes full weed-suppressing canopy in 3–4 weeks and decomposes readily after termination.

crops.rootSystem: Fine branched root system highly efficient at phosphorus mobilization in low-P topsoil.

growingWindow.planting: July–August (late summer catch cover) or May–June
growingWindow.description: Fast-growing Polygonaceae summer/autumn cover and break crop widely documented in China (North, Northwest, and Southwest), Europe, and North America.

diseasePestNotes: Non-host to cereal cyst nematodes, SCN, clubroot, and take-all.
Attracts beneficial hoverflies and predatory insects that reduce aphid pressure in subsequent crops.
